claim: Axons contain a smooth tubular endoplasmic reticulum (ER) network that is thought to be continuous with ER throughout the neuron.
source: Axons contain a smooth tubular endoplasmic reticulum (ER) network that is thought to be continuous with ER throughout the neuron
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on ER continuity in neurons

claim: Mutations affecting reticulon or REEP proteins cause hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), an axon degenerative disease.
source: Mutations affecting reticulon or REEP proteins, with intramembrane hairpin domains that model ER membranes, cause an axon degenerative disease, hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript

claim: Drosophila axons have a dynamic axonal ER network.
source: We show that Drosophila axons have a dynamic axonal ER network, which these proteins help to model.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations including live imaging data shown in Figure 5

claim: Loss of HSP hairpin proteins causes ER sheet expansion in Drosophila.
source: Loss of HSP hairpin proteins causes ER sheet expansion, partial loss of ER from distal motor axons, and occasional discontinuities in axonal ER.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 7

claim: Loss of HSP hairpin proteins causes partial loss of ER from distal motor axons.
source: Loss of HSP hairpin proteins causes ER sheet expansion, partial loss of ER from distal motor axons, and occasional discontinuities in axonal ER.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: Loss of HSP hairpin proteins causes occasional discontinuities in axonal ER.
source: Loss of HSP hairpin proteins causes ER sheet expansion, partial loss of ER from distal motor axons, and occasional discontinuities in axonal ER.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy and EM data shown in Figures 4, 5, and 7

claim: Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutant larvae show larger and fewer ER tubules in axons compared to wild-type.
source: Ultrastructural analysis reveals an extensive ER network in axons, which shows larger and fewer tubules in larvae that lack reticulon and REEP proteins, consistent with loss of membrane curvature.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 7B-E

claim: HSP hairpin-containing proteins are required for shaping and continuity of axonal ER.
source: Therefore HSP hairpin-containing proteins are required for shaping and continuity of axonal ER, thus suggesting roles for ER modeling in axon maintenance and function.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations including confocal microscopy, FRAP, and EM data

claim: Axonal ER appears mostly tubular and smooth, with some cisternae.
source: Axonal ER appears mostly tubular and smooth, with some cisternae (Tsukita and Ishikawa, 1976; Lindsey and Ellisman, 1985; Villegas et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior ultrastructural studies

claim: Numerous mRNAs are found in both growing and mature axons.
source: numerous mRNAs are found in both growing and mature axons (Zivraj et al., 2010; Shigeoka et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Local axonal translation can occur in response to injury.
source: local axonal translation can occur in response to injury (Ben-Yaakov et al., 2012; Perry et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Rough ER sheets and markers of protein export and folding are relatively sparse in mature axons.
source: However, rough ER sheets (Tsukita and Ishikawa, 1976; Villegas et al., 2014), and markers of protein export and folding that are characteristic of rough ER (Röper, 2007; O'Sullivan et al., 2012), are relatively sparse in mature axons.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies including authors' own work

claim: Axonal ER likely has major roles in lipid biosynthesis, calcium homeostasis and signaling, and coordination of organelle physiology.
source: Axonal ER therefore likely has major roles other than protein export; these could include lipid biosynthesis (Tidhar and Futerman, 2013; Vance, 2015), calcium homeostasis and signaling (Ross, 2012), and coordination of organelle physiology (Phillips and Voeltz, 2016).
evidence: Speculative inference based on known ER functions and citations

claim: An ER-dependent propagating calcium wave is seen after axotomy of C. elegans or mammalian dorsal root ganglion neurons.
source: indeed, an ER-dependent propagating calcium wave is seen after axotomy of Caenorhabditis elegans or mammalian dorsal root ganglion neurons (Ghosh-Roy et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies

claim: Mutations affecting spastin, atlastin-1, reticulon-2, REEP1 and REEP2 account for most cases of autosomal dominant 'pure' HSP.
source: Mutations affecting spastin, atlastin-1, reticulon-2, REEP1 and REEP2 account for most cases of autosomal dominant 'pure' HSP (Hazan et al., 1999; Zhao et al., 2001; Züchner et al., 2006; Montenegro et al., 2012; Esteves et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior genetic studies

claim: REEP and reticulon family proteins share a common feature of one or two hydrophobic hairpin-loops inserted in the ER membrane.
source: These proteins share a common feature of one or two hydrophobic hairpin-loops inserted in the ER membrane, promoting ER membrane curvature in a process termed hydrophobic wedging (Voeltz et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior structural/biochemical work

claim: REEP and reticulon proteins promote ER membrane curvature through hydrophobic wedging.
source: These proteins share a common feature of one or two hydrophobic hairpin-loops inserted in the ER membrane, promoting ER membrane curvature in a process termed hydrophobic wedging (Voeltz et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior mechanistic work

claim: REEP and reticulon family proteins localize preferentially to tubular or smooth ER.
source: Proteins of the REEP and reticulon families localize preferentially to tubular or smooth ER, and their loss results in disruption of ER tubular organization (Shibata et al., 2006; Voeltz et al., 2006; Park et al., 2010; Shibata et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior localization studies

claim: Loss of REEP and reticulon proteins results in disruption of ER tubular organization.
source: Proteins of the REEP and reticulon families localize preferentially to tubular or smooth ER, and their loss results in disruption of ER tubular organization (Shibata et al., 2006; Voeltz et al., 2006; Park et al., 2010; Shibata et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior functional studies

claim: REEP and reticulon proteins may contribute to modeling of rough ER sheets by stabilizing their curved edges.
source: they may also contribute to modeling of rough ER sheets by stabilizing their curved edges (Shibata et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculative claim supported by citation

claim: HSP-causing mutations often appear to cause loss of protein expression or function.
source: HSP-causing mutations often appear to cause loss of protein expression or function (Beetz et al., 2013; Novarino et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior genetic/functional studies

claim: The ability of hairpin-loop proteins to form homomeric and heteromeric complexes allows some point mutations to have dominant negative effects.
source: the ability of hairpin-loop proteins to form homomeric and heteromeric complexes (Shibata et al., 2008) allows some point mutations to have dominant negative effects (Züchner et al., 2006; Beetz et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior biochemical and genetic studies

claim: Reticulon and REEP family proteins are redundantly required for most peripheral ER tubules in yeast.
source: Since reticulon and REEP family proteins are redundantly required for most peripheral ER tubules in yeast (Voeltz et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior yeast genetic study

claim: Knockdown of Drosophila reticulon Rtnl1 causes expansion of epidermal ER sheets.
source: We previously showed that knockdown of the Drosophila reticulon Rtnl1 causes expansion of epidermal ER sheets, and partial loss of smooth ER marker from distal but not proximal motor axons (O'Sullivan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' prior work

claim: Knockdown of Drosophila reticulon Rtnl1 causes partial loss of smooth ER marker from distal but not proximal motor axons.
source: We previously showed that knockdown of the Drosophila reticulon Rtnl1 causes expansion of epidermal ER sheets, and partial loss of smooth ER marker from distal but not proximal motor axons (O'Sullivan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' prior work

claim: CG42678 is the single Drosophila ortholog of mammalian REEP1-REEP4.
source: Multiple sequence alignment of mammalian and Drosophila REEP protein sequences suggested that CG42678 was the single Drosophila ortholog of mammalian REEP1-REEP4 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: Mammalian REEP5 and REEP6 share two Drosophila orthologs, CG8331 and CG4960.
source: Mammalian REEP5 and REEP6 appeared to share two Drosophila orthologs, CG8331 and CG4960 (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1

claim: ReepA1::GFP and ReepB::GFP overlap with anti-KDEL labeling in larval epidermal cells.
source: Overlap of ReepA1::GFP and ReepB::GFP with anti-KDEL labeling in larval epidermal cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 1E

claim: ReepB::GFP is more strongly expressed in third instar larval CNS than ReepA3::GFP.
source: ReepB::GFP was also more strongly expressed in third instar larval CNS than ReepA3::GFP, which was the only ReepA::GFP fusion that we detected there (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 1F

claim: ReepB::GFP localizes continuously along the length of peripheral nerves.
source: A single confocal section of a peripheral nerve, showing ReepB::GFP localized continuously along its length.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 1G

claim: ReepB::GFP localizes as a mostly continual structure along the length of presynaptic terminals of neuromuscular junctions.
source: ReepB::GFP, but none of the ReepA::GFP fusions, localized as a mostly continual structure along the length of presynaptic terminals of neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 1H,I

claim: Rtnl1− mutant larvae show loss of ER network organization in epidermal cells.
source: Rtnl1− mutant larvae also showed loss of ER network organization (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 2A

claim: Intensity of KDEL labeling fluctuates less in Rtnl1− larvae compared to wild-type.
source: Intensity of KDEL labeling along a line from the nucleus to cell periphery displayed fluctuating intensity, reflecting the reticular distribution of KDEL in wild-type larvae, but less fluctuation in Rtnl1− larvae
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of confocal images in Figure 2A

claim: Loss of both ReepA and ReepB makes KDEL levels in larval epidermal cells fluctuate less than in controls.
source: Similarly, loss of both ReepA and ReepB, but not loss of either gene alone, made KDEL levels in larval epidermal cells fluctuate less than in controls.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of confocal images in Figure 2B

claim: ReepA− ReepB− double mutant epidermal cells show longer ribosome studded sheet ER profiles compared to controls.
source: This revealed that ReepA− ReepB− double mutant epidermal cells showed longer ribosome studded sheet ER profiles, compared to controls, and to ReepA− and ReepB− single mutants (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy measurements in Figure 2C

claim: ReepA− ReepB− mutants show increased ER stress in epidermal cells but not in CNS.
source: ReepA− ReepB− mutants also showed increased ER stress in epidermal cells (Figure 2D) but not in CNS (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by Xbp1::GFP reporter expression in Figure 2D,E

claim: Loss of Rtnl1 causes partial loss of Acsl::myc from posterior axons but not from anterior axons.
source: Loss of Rtnl1 caused partial loss of Acsl::myc from posterior (segment A6) axons, but not from anterior axons (segment A2)
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 3A

claim: Loss of Rtnl1 causes Acsl::myc staining to appear more irregular in posterior but not anterior axons.
source: it also caused Acsl::myc staining to appear more irregular in posterior but not anterior axons, reflected in a higher coefficient of variation (SD/mean) of Acsl::myc staining intensity along the length of posterior axons lacking Rtnl1, compared to wild-type (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of confocal images in Figure 3A

claim: The Rtnl1− mutant phenotypes can be partially rescued by one copy of an Rtnl1Pacman genomic clone.
source: the Rtnl1− mutant phenotypes could be partially rescued by one copy of an Rtnl1Pacman genomic clone (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic rescue experiment shown in Figure 3A

claim: ReepB− mutants show partial loss of Acsl::myc from posterior but not anterior motor axons.
source: Similar to Rtnl1 loss of function, ReepB− mutants showed partial loss of Acsl::myc from posterior but not anterior motor axons (Figure 3B)
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 3B

claim: The ReepB− phenotype can be mostly rescued by one copy of a genomic ReepB::GFP clone.
source: this phenotype was partially rescued with one copy of a genomic ReepB::GFP clone, and was also observed on ReepB knockdown in m12-GAL4-expressing neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic rescue experiment shown in Figure 3B

claim: ReepA− mutants show no loss of Acsl::myc from axons.
source: ReepA− mutants showed no loss of Acsl::myc from axons.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 3B

claim: A ReepA− ReepB− double mutant shows loss of Acsl::myc from posterior axons similar to ReepB− mutants.
source: A ReepA− ReepB− double mutant showed loss of Acsl::myc from posterior axons, that was similar to that seen in ReepB− mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 3B

claim: ReepA− ReepB− double mutant larvae show increased coefficient of variation of Acsl::myc staining intensity in posterior but not anterior axons.
source: ReepA− ReepB− double mutant larvae, but not ReepA− single mutants, showed an increased coefficient of variation of Acsl::myc staining intensity in posterior but not in anterior axons
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of confocal images in Figure 3B

claim: Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutants are viable and fertile as adults.
source: Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutants were viable and fertile as adults, but survived poorly beyond two weeks of adulthood, compared to 4–5 weeks for wild-type adults.
evidence: Observed phenotype from maintaining fly stocks

claim: Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutants survive poorly beyond two weeks of adulthood, compared to 4–5 weeks for wild-type adults.
source: Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutants were viable and fertile as adults, but survived poorly beyond two weeks of adulthood, compared to 4–5 weeks for wild-type adults.
evidence: Observed phenotype from maintaining fly stocks

claim: Triple mutant larvae show increased fluctuation of Acsl::myc staining intensity along motor axons compared to wild-type, mainly in middle parts of longer axons.
source: Triple mutant larvae showed increased fluctuation of Acsl::myc staining intensity along motor axons compared to wild-type, mainly in middle parts (segment A4 and A5) of longer axons.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 4

claim: At its most extreme, increased fluctuation of Acsl::myc manifests as fragmentation of Acsl::myc labeling in triple mutant axons, which is never seen in wild-type axons.
source: At its most extreme, this manifested as fragmentation of Acsl::myc labeling, which was never seen in wild-type axons (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 4A,B

claim: When gaps in labeling are found in the central regions of axons, labeling in the anterior and posterior parts of the same axons is usually continuous.
source: When gaps in labeling were found in the central regions of axons, labeling in the anterior and posterior parts of the same axons was usually continuous (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 4A

claim: Double labeling shows no effect on axonal plasma membrane in Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutant compared to control axons.
source: Double labeling of plasma membrane (CD4::tdGFP) and axonal ER (Acsl::myc) showed no effect on axonal plasma membrane in Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutant compared to control axons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The ER fragmentation phenotype is limited to ER and does not affect axon integrity.
source: implying that the phenotype was limited to ER and did not affect axon integrity.
evidence: Inferred from plasma membrane labeling data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Rtnl1 loss-of-function axons show a mild ER fragmentation phenotype.
source: Rtnl1 loss-of-function axons, but not ReepA− ReepB− mutant axons, also showed a mild ER fragmentation phenotype (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 4A,B

claim: ReepA− ReepB− mutant axons do not show an ER fragmentation phenotype.
source: Rtnl1 loss-of-function axons, but not ReepA− ReepB− mutant axons, also showed a mild ER fragmentation phenotype (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 4A,B

claim: Rtnl1(RNAi) ReepA− ReepB− larvae show a fragmentation phenotype similar to Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB−, suggesting that loss of Rtnl1 is essential for it.
source: Rtnl1(RNAi) ReepA− ReepB− larvae also showed a fragmentation phenotype similar to Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB−, suggesting that loss of Rtnl1 is essential for it (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 4B, with inference about Rtnl1 requirement

claim: Rtnl1− ReepB− double mutant axons show a similar phenotype to Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutants.
source: Rtnl1− ReepB− double mutant axons also showed a similar phenotype to Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 4

claim: Loss of Rtnl1 causes irregular organization of axonal ER, and this phenotype is exacerbated by loss of ReepB, with no detectable contribution of ReepA loss.
source: Therefore, loss of Rtnl1 causes a mild irregular organization of axonal ER, and this phenotype is exacerbated by loss of ReepB, with no detectable contribution of ReepA loss
evidence: Inferred from comparison of multiple genotypes in Figure 4

claim: CG9186::GFP, Rtnl1::GFP and tdTomato::Sec61β all localize to ER and show continuous labeling in wild-type axons.
source: The lipase CG9186::GFP (Thiel et al., 2013), Rtnl1::GFP (Rao et al., 2016) and tdTomato::Sec61β (Summerville et al., 2016) all localize to ER, and all showed continuous labeling in wild-type (ReepA+) axons (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: CG9186::GFP shows occasional gaps in triple mutant axons.
source: However, CG9186::GFP showed occasional gaps in triple mutant axons (Figure 5A), with at least one gap per larva visible by confocal microscopy in 6/17 larvae.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 5A

claim: After bleaching a 12 µm length of axon in either wild-type or triple mutant axons lacking gaps, rapid recovery of fluorescence from both ends of the bleached region is observed.
source: After bleaching a 12 µm length of axon in either wild-type axons or in Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutant axons lacking gaps, we observed rapid recovery of fluorescence from both ends of the bleached region (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Video 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by FRAP experiments in Figure 5 and Video 1

claim: The kinetics of fluorescence recovery after photobleaching are similar between wildtype and triple mutant axons lacking gaps.
source: The kinetics of recovery were similar between wildtype and triple mutant axons (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative FRAP analysis in Figure 5B-D

claim: In regions next to gaps in CG9186::GFP labeling in triple mutant axons, good recovery of fluorescence from the end opposite the gap is observed, but no recovery across the gap.
source: We also performed FRAP on regions next to gaps in CG9186::GFP labeling in triple mutant axons (Figure 5A); here we observed good recovery of fluorescence from the end of the bleached region opposite the gap, but no recovery across the gap (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Videos 2–4)
evidence: Demonstrated by FRAP experiments in Figure 5 and Videos 2-4

claim: Gaps in CG9186::GFP labelling are physical barriers to diffusion of CG9186::GFP, and hence gaps in the ER network.
source: suggesting that gaps in CG9186::GFP labelling were also physical barriers to diffusion of CG9186::GFP, and hence gaps in the ER network.
evidence: Inferred from FRAP experiments showing no recovery across gaps

claim: Features such as higher or lower levels of CG9186::GFP labelling are mostly stable throughout a 200 s acquisition period.
source: Features such as higher or lower levels of CG9186::GFP labelling (which could reflect variation in the numbers of tubules, or the presence of structures like cisternae) were mostly stable throughout a 200 s acquisition period (Figure 5A,E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by live imaging in Figure 5A,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Anterograde or retrograde movement of more brightly labeled ER regions is observed during live imaging.
source: However, we also observed some dynamic features, including anterograde or retrograde movement of more brightly labeled regions (Figure 5A,E) perhaps representing movement of ER tubules detached from the ER network
evidence: Demonstrated by live imaging in Figure 5A,E

claim: Retrograde movement of labeled puncta at around 0.3 µm/s is observed during live imaging.
source: and retrograde movement of labeled puncta (Figure 5E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Video 3), at around 0.3 µm/s.
evidence: Demonstrated by live imaging and kymograph analysis in Figure 5E

claim: Most gaps in ER labeling in triple mutants are stable over 200 s (7 out of 8 gaps imaged).
source: While most gaps in ER labeling in triple mutants were stable over 200 s (7 out of 8 gaps imaged, including Videos 2–3)
evidence: Demonstrated by live imaging observations

claim: In one case, a gap was closed up by anterograde movement of a 5 µm length of ER proximal to the gap, which simultaneously opened up a new gap proximal to the moving section.
source: in one case a gap was closed up by anterograde movement of a 5 µm length of ER proximal to the gap, which simultaneously opened up a new gap proximal to the moving section (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Video 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by live imaging in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and Video 4

claim: In one case, a labeled punctum moved retrogradely across an ER gap without pausing, implying that microtubule-based transport was intact.
source: In one case a labeled punctum moved retrogradely across an ER gap without pausing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), implying that microtubule-based transport was intact.
evidence: Demonstrated by live imaging in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, with inference about transport

claim: ER is normally continuous in axons.
source: Therefore, live imaging and photobleaching of CG9186::GFP both suggest that ER is normally continuous in axons
evidence: Inferred from FRAP and live imaging data in Figure 5

claim: Loss of reticulon and REEP proteins leads to occasional gaps in ER labeling that represent physical breaks of ER continuity.
source: that loss of reticulon and REEP proteins leads to occasional gaps in ER labeling that represent physical breaks of ER continuity
evidence: Inferred from FRAP experiments showing no recovery across gaps

claim: ER network organization in axons shows both static and dynamic features.
source: and that ER network organization in axons shows both static and dynamic features.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations in Figure 5

claim: Rtnl1− larvae and Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutant larvae show large accumulations of CSP in many peripheral nerves.
source: Rtnl1− larvae and Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutant larvae showed large accumulations of CSP in many peripheral nerves.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 6

claim: The large accumulations of CSP in Rtnl1− larvae can be rescued by two copies of a Rtnl1Pacman genomic clone.
source: The large accumulations of CSP in Rtnl1− larvae could be rescued by two copies of a Rtnl1Pacman genomic clone (Figure 6).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic rescue experiment in Figure 6

claim: Wild-type larvae show a network of ER tubules in every axon that could be observed.
source: Wild-type larvae showed a network of ER tubules, in every axon that could be observed (Figure 7A left; serial sections in Video 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy in Figure 7A and Video 5

claim: ER tubule outer diameter in wild-type axons averages around 40 nm.
source: Tubule outer diameter averaged around 40 nm (Figure 7B,C)
evidence: Measured from electron microscopy images in Figure 7B,C

claim: Wild-type axons contain an average of around 1.6 ER tubules in each cross-section.
source: and axons contained an average of around 1.6 ER tubules in each cross-section (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Measured from electron microscopy images in Figure 7D,E

claim: 3D reconstruction shows a tubular ER network with multiple branches, some dead ends, and continuity along nearly every axon sectioned.

claim: ER tubules often show proximity to mitochondria or plasma membrane in wild-type axons.
source: ER tubules often showed proximity to mitochondria or plasma membrane (Figure 7G left).

claim: Occasional structures resembling small patches of ER sheets with an adjoining cisterna are found in wild-type axons, continuous with the tubular ER network, at a frequency averaging around one per 20 µm per axon.
source: We also found occasional structures resembling small patches of ER sheets with an adjoining cisterna (Figure 7H), continuous with the tubular ER network (Video 6), at a frequency averaging around one per 20 µm per axon.

claim: ER tubule diameter is increased to around 60 nm in Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− triple mutant axons.
source: ER tubule diameter was increased to around 60 nm (Figure 7B,C)

claim: A lumen can be seen in some ER tubules in triple mutant axons, which is rarely seen in wild-type.
source: allowing a lumen to be seen in some tubules (Figure 7A right; Video 7) that was rarely seen in wild-type (Figure 7A left; Video 5)

claim: Most triple mutant axons exhibit only a single ER tubule per cross-section.
source: and most triple mutant axons exhibited only a single ER tubule (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Measured from electron microscopy images in Figure 7D,E

claim: Reconstructions show a less extensive ER network in mutant axons compared to wild-type.
source: Reconstructions (Figure 7F right; Supplementary file 3) showed a less extensive ER network in mutant axons.

claim: Frequent contacts of ER with mitochondria and plasma membrane are found in both wild-type and Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− mutant axons.
source: Frequent contacts of ER with mitochondria and plasma membrane were found in both wild-type and Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− mutant axons (Figure 7G).

claim: Both wild-type and mutant axons show swellings containing mitochondria and clusters of vesicles resembling synaptic vesicles.
source: Both wild-type and mutant axons showed swellings containing mitochondria and clusters of vesicles resembling synaptic vesicles (Figure 7I; Video 8).

claim: Some discontinuity of the ER network is observed in about 10% of wild-type or Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− mutant axons.
source: Some discontinuity of the ER network was observed in about 10% of wild-type or Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− mutant axons (Figure 7L).

claim: Gaps in Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− mutant axons are longer than in wild-type axons.
source: However, gaps in Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− mutant axons (Figure 7J,K; Video 9; Supplementary file 4) were longer (Figure 7M)

claim: Gaps in Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− mutant axons are slightly more numerous than in wild-type, but not significantly when averaged across larvae.
source: and slightly more numerous (but not significantly when averaged across larvae; Figure 7N) than in wild-type axons

claim: The length of affected axons that lack ER tubules is nearly four-fold increased in Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− mutants compared to wild-type.
source: resulting in nearly a four-fold increase in the length of affected axons that lacked ER tubules (Figure 7O).

claim: All glial classes, but particularly subperineurial glia, show a trend towards increased ER sheet profile length in Rtnl1− ReepA− ReepB− mutant nerves compared to control.

claim: Triple mutant wrapping glia display more extensive wrapping, sometimes completely ensheathing axons, which is rarely observed in control nerve sections.
source: Triple mutant wrapping glia also displayed more extensive wrapping, sometimes completely ensheathing axons, which was rarely observed in control nerve sections (Figure 8J–M; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy in Figure 8J-M and Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: The tubular ER network is highly dynamic in non-neuronal cells.
source: The tubular ER network is highly dynamic in non-neuronal cells (Nixon-Abell et al., 2016; Valm et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: In axons, live imaging suggests dynamic features superimposed on a structure that is largely stable over 1–2 min of imaging.
source: and in axons our live imaging suggests dynamic features superimposed on a structure that is largely stable over the 1–2 min of imaging (Figure 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by live imaging data in Figure 5

claim: ER tubules are effectively ubiquitous in Drosophila peripheral nerve sections.

claim: Reconstruction over several µm shows a continuous network of ER tubules in most axons examined.
source: Reconstruction over several µm showed a continuous network of ER tubules in most axons examined, in agreement with the ER continuity found in neurons by lipid dye labeling (Terasaki et al., 1994), and recently in reconstructions of serial sections from focused ion beam SEM (Wu et al., 2017).

claim: In a few axons, short lengths of axon with no detectable ER are found.
source: However, in a few axons, we found short lengths of axon with no detectable ER (Figure 7J–O).

claim: Larger ER tubules could potentially store and release more calcium than thinner ones.
source: Larger tubules could potentially store and release more calcium than thinner ones
